chapter.name: Trigonometric Functions
chapter.blurb: This chapter measures angles in degrees and radians, links arc length to the angle at the centre by l = r theta, and extends the trigonometric ratios of acute angles to trigonometric functions of any real number using the unit circle. It studies the signs, domain, range, behaviour and graphs of the six functions and how to find their values in any quadrant. It then builds the identities for sums and differences of angles, double and triple angles, and the conversion between sums and products.

concepts.name: Angles: degree measure, radian measure and conversion
concepts.description: Positive and negative angles, degrees-minutes-seconds, the radian as a unit, and conversion between degrees and radians using pi radians = 180 degrees.
concepts.idea: An angle measures the rotation of a ray about its initial point: anticlockwise is positive, clockwise is negative. It can be measured in degrees (1/360 of a revolution) or in radians (the angle subtended at the centre of a unit circle by an arc of length 1 unit).
concepts.rule: pi radians = 180 degrees. Radian measure = (pi/180) x degree measure; degree measure = (180/pi) x radian measure. 1 degree = 60 minutes and 1 minute = 60 seconds.
concepts.example: 40 degrees 20 minutes = 121/3 degrees = (pi/180) x (121/3) = 121 pi/540 radians.

concepts.idea: In a circle of radius r an arc of length r subtends 1 radian at the centre, and equal arcs subtend equal angles, so an arc of length l subtends l/r radians.

concepts.name: Unit-circle definitions, standard values and basic identities
concepts.description: sin x and cos x as coordinates of a point on the unit circle, the other four functions and where they are undefined, values at quadrantal and standard angles, zeros of sine and cosine, and the three square identities.
concepts.idea: For a point P(a, b) on the unit circle with arc AP = x, cos x = a and sin x = b. The other four functions are built from these as quotients and reciprocals, so they fail to exist where the denominator is zero.
concepts.rule: sin^2 x + cos^2 x = 1, 1 + tan^2 x = sec^2 x, 1 + cot^2 x = cosec^2 x. sin x = 0 implies x = n pi; cos x = 0 implies x = (2n + 1) pi/2. sin (2n pi + x) = sin x and cos (2n pi + x) = cos x.

questions.q: For each of the quadrantal angles x = 0, pi/2, pi and 3 pi/2, determine which of the six trigonometric functions are not defined, and explain the pattern you find.
questions.a: At x = 0 and x = pi, sin x = 0 (points (1, 0) and (-1, 0)), so cosec x = 1/sin x and cot x = cos x/sin x are not defined, while sin, cos, tan and sec are defined. At x = pi/2 and x = 3 pi/2, cos x = 0 (points (0, 1) and (0, -1)), so sec x = 1/cos x and tan x = sin x/cos x are not defined, while sin, cos, cosec and cot are defined. Pattern: at every quadrantal angle exactly two functions are undefined - those with sin x in the denominator at multiples of pi, and those with cos x in the denominator at odd multiples of pi/2; sin and cos themselves are always defined.

At x = pi/2 (and every odd multiple of pi/2) neither side is defined, so the identity makes no claim there; that does not make it false. For example, at x = pi/4, 1 + 1 = 2 = (sqrt(2))^2.
s: States that the identity holds wherever tan x and sec x are defined (cos x not zero)
Explains that x = pi/2 lies outside the domain of both sides, so it is not a counter-example

s: Writes cos 6x = 4 cos^3 2x - 3 cos 2x using the triple-angle formula
Substitutes cos 2x = 2 cos^2 x - 1 and expands the cube correctly

questions.q: Develop a formula that expresses cos 4x in terms of cos x only, and test your formula at x = pi/3.

Test at x = pi/3: cos x = 1/2, so the formula gives 8/16 - 8/4 + 1 = 1/2 - 2 + 1 = -1/2. Directly, cos (4 pi/3) = cos (pi + pi/3) = -cos (pi/3) = -1/2. The two agree.
s: Applies the double-angle formula twice: cos 4x = 2 cos^2 2x - 1 with cos 2x = 2 cos^2 x - 1
Expands to cos 4x = 8 cos^4 x - 8 cos^2 x + 1
Tests at x = pi/3 and gets -1/2 both ways

concepts.name: Sum-to-product and product-to-sum identities
concepts.description: The four identities turning cos x + cos y, cos x - cos y, sin x + sin y and sin x - sin y into products, the four reverse identities for 2 cos x cos y, -2 sin x sin y, 2 sin x cos y and 2 cos x sin y, and their use in simplifying and proving identities.
concepts.idea: Adding and subtracting the formulas for x + y and x - y gives products as sums; renaming x + y and x - y turns sums into products with half the sum and half the difference of the angles.
concepts.rule: cos x + cos y = 2 cos ((x + y)/2) cos ((x - y)/2); cos x - cos y = -2 sin ((x + y)/2) sin ((x - y)/2); sin x + sin y = 2 sin ((x + y)/2) cos ((x - y)/2); sin x - sin y = 2 cos ((x + y)/2) sin ((x - y)/2).
concepts.example: (cos 7x + cos 5x)/(sin 7x - sin 5x) = (2 cos 6x cos x)/(2 cos 6x sin x) = cot x.

questions.q: Prove that (sin 5x - 2 sin 3x + sin x)/(cos 5x - cos x) = tan x.

So the left side is 2 sin 3x (cos 2x - 1)/(-2 sin 3x sin 2x) = (1 - cos 2x)/sin 2x. Using 1 - cos 2x = 2 sin^2 x and sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x, this is 2 sin^2 x/(2 sin x cos x) = tan x.

(Other valid choices: a = 6, b = 4 or a = 8, b = 2 or a = 9, b = 1.)

Applies both sum-to-product identities and cancels to get tan 5x
